subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESERVE IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESERVE IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house of some
recent developments in Indian affairs. It is recognized that many Indian communities do not have adequate homes, either in quality or in number, and that many reserves lack facilities and services such as electricity, running water, bathrooms, sewage disposal systems or good roads.
I am pleased to inform the house that an extensive Indian reserve improvement program, to cost about $112 million in the next five years, will be undertaken. Under the program Indians will receive assistance to provide better housing, safe water supply, sanitation facilities, electrification of homes and improved roads in their communities.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
A comprehensive study of housing conditions on reserves was completed in February, 1965, indicating a need for 12,000 new houses over the next five years to meet the backlog of approximately 6,000 houses required now, and new family formations of about 1,250 a year. In addition, community services are required on many reserves.
Many of the Indian leaders, as well as others, have been suggesting what would amount to a crash program to raise living conditions in Indian communities, particularly housing. The situation was discussed with the national Indian advisory board which met in Ottawa from January 10 to 12 this year. The board called for an accelerated program to eliminate the problem in the shortest time.
Under the accelerated program the objective is to build 12,000 houses in five years. Apart from what may be met from band funds and personal contributions, about $75 million in public funds will be required. The program will be flexible to meet the wide variety of reserve conditions across Canada, but will recognize four general areas of need:
First, there are those who are widowed, aged, indigent, disabled, or otherwise unable to make more than a token contribution toward their homes. Suitable housing will be provided for them largely at public expense.
Second, there are those Indian families living in marginal economic areas who must be helped in some way to provide homes for their families which are of minimum standards for decent living.
March 17, 1966
2802	COMMONS DEBATES
Indian Reserve Improvement Program
Third, .there are those Indian families who live on reserves where economic conditions and prospects are favourable, where through wages or self employment they earn sufficient income to be able to contribute to the cost of their homes. Some assistance will be provided to enable them to acquire a higher standard of home.
Fourth, there are Indian families who wish to take advantage of employment opportunities off the reserve and may even wish to live permanently off the reserve. In order to help these families to obtain and hold jobs away from the reserve, financial assistance will be provided so they will be able to take advantage of normal lending facilities available to Canadians generally for the purchase of homes.
The expanded housing program, therefore, is intended to provide support to Indian families not only to obtain reasonably satisfactory houses but also to upgrade the level of Indian housing across Canada. Of great importance is the supply of safe drinking water and proper sewage disposal. Vast improvements in this field are needed if Indian people are to have the advantages enjoyed by most Canadians. Some $10 million will be spent for this purpose.
It is quite evident that progress on many reserves has been seriously hampered by the lack of electricity. It is necessary to bring electricity to reserves if Indian children are to obtain full advantage from the school program, and if the amenities of life are to be made available and economic opportunities are to be furthered. Power is essential to so many of the facilities we use daily and take for granted. Therefore a rural electrification program will be undertaken using existing public utilities wherever possible. The cost of this program over the next five years is expected to be $7 million and will be directed mainly to communities where Indians lack band funds necessary to extend facilities.
Transportation is of vital importance to provide access to and from reserves, for school children, employment opportunities and economic development. Improved roads on many reserves are a necessity. To this end some $17 million will be spent in co-operation with Indian band councils and other levels of government.
In order to achieve the best results from the expenditure of public funds it is necessary to co-ordinate all aspects of the reserve improvement program. Community planning is essential. This has been undertaken on a

number of reserves, and scores of other communities will be examined as the needs and priorities are considered and established by the Indian communities.
Of particular importance-and on which in large measure the success of the program will depend-is the total involvement and participation of Indian band councils and the Indian people themselves.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESERVE IMPROVEMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this is the first major announcement on Indian affairs policy that has been made by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources in the house since he assumed responsibility for this important department. As I listened to his presentation, Mr. Speaker, it seemed to me that there was a strong northern affairs influence in the policy he outlined.
It is well known to all members of this house as well as to the people of Canada generally that one of our most neglected groups, and one of the most neglected areas of social responsibility in Canada has been in the realm of our attitude toward what we sometimes refer to euphemistically as our first Canadians.
It is encouraging to note that in the past few months there has been an upsurge of public interest in this question which is now reflected in the anouncement which has just been made by the minister of northern affairs.
Housing, of course, in Canada is one of our basic problems. That is why the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources gave primary consideration to the needs of the Eskimo population in this connection. In more recent years there has been a problem of increasing proportions, in that good housing programs were available for our Eskimo population but at the same time our Indian population was sadly neglected.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that with this program announced by the minister the two groups will now be able to move along parallel lines. What the minister proposes will mean a tremendous improvement in the family and community life of our Indian people.
We must, of course, recognize that a house is not necessarily a home. I am glad to see that the minister has included in the basic housing program the necessary services and amenities which provide for a reasonable standard of living. I refer of course to amenities such as power, water, sewerage, and the necessary access roads.
March 17. 1966

All this is a good beginning. I would point out to the minister that several of the provinces have seized the initiative in dealing with the larger problems of our Indian population, and have taken leadership in the community development concept. If we are going to really rehabilitate our Indian reservations, which exist at the present time largely as depressed ghettos, I think we have to expand as rapidly as possible the community development concept which makes it possible for the people on the reserves to have a sense of belonging to a community. When our Indian people have that sense of belonging it will give to them that initiative and that motivation to improve which is so necessary to them, as they have lived under the cloud of paternalism for too long.
I trust that in administering this program, Mr. Speaker, we will not forget the special housing needs of Indians off the reserve. I think I detected a hint in this direction when the minister suggested that the special housing needs of our Canadian Indians who are moving away from the reserve system will be taken into consideration. Those people are not able to qualify under the terms of the Central Mortgage and Housing program at the moment, and this fact has constituted a discouraging factor in preventing them from moving into a position of responsibility and equality in the larger Canadian community.
I congratulate the government for taking the initiative in this program. It has been recommended by the National Indian Council for years, and more recently by the newly formed Indian Advisory Council. I should also like to pay tribute to the Indian-Eskimo Association, which has had its eye on this target for the past number of years. I hope it is the beginning of a more dynamic, broader approach to all the basic social problems of our first Canadians.

I think there is no doubt but that the minister is to be congratulated on this move which is being made to correct some of the abuse under which our native Indian population has suffered ever since the white man came to the country. While I commend the minister for the action he has taken, action

Indian Reserve Improvement Program which is long overdue, I hope he will not take it as a criticism of that action when I suggest there are still many things which need to be done.

In the first place, I wish he could have expanded on the question of Indian education. I think we should have some idea of the government's policy in this field. I realize there are difficulties with regard to jurisdiction where education is concerned, but I think the department should make every effort to encourage the attendance of Indian children at our public schools and to integrate them into the population. To this end I believe arrangements should be made with the local school authorities concerning school attendance, the provision of transportation and so on.
Another matter which I believe should be brought to the attention of the minister is this. The level of welfare and social assistance now granted to Indians by the federal authority is greatly below the level of social assistance granted by the provinces, at least by my own province of British Columbia and I imagine by other provinces too. It has long been a sore point with Indians that they are not eligible for the same level of social assistance and welfare aid as their white compatriots.
Something else occurs to me. While it is commendable to make every effort to see that our native population is well housed, we should also realize that the best of houses is inadequate if there is no income upon which to maintain it. There are areas in my own province where there are no employment opportunities of any particular value in close proximity to the Indian reserves, and I wonder whether the minister might not consider sponsoring or initiating the development of employment possibilities on or close to these reserves.
Before I sit down I think it is proper to do something I had intended to do at another point in our proceedings, that is to comment on the death yesterday of an extremely eminent member of our native Indian population, Rev. speakeroldname: Mr. D. S. Macdonald (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. CROIX RIVER BRIDGE STRUCTURE TO CONNECT NEW BRUNSWICK AND MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think hon. members will find Bill No. S-15 to be relatively straightforward and therefore no additional statement of great length should be required at this time. However, I will make available to hon. members one or two further details which will not appear from the bill itself.
The government of the province of New Brunswick wishes to build this bridge between the town of Milltown, New Brunswick, and the city of Calais in Maine. This, of course, would be an international bridge between Canada and the United States. Under the provisions of section 92 (10) (a) of the British North America Act, this will be a work extending beyond the limits of one province and therefore it is a work falling under the authority of the parliament of Canada. For this reason the province of New Brunswick has come to this parliament to receive authorization for the construction of the work.
The bridge will be constructed, operated and maintained by the government of the province of New Brunswick in co-operation with the government of the state of Maine. Each of these governments would pay half of the cost of constructing the bridge and the entire cost of all approach works and right of way within its own borders. The two governments would share the cost of maintenance and operation of the bridge once it is completed on the same equal basis. The federal government would make no financial contribution to the bridge and it is intended that the bridge should be toll free.
March 17, 1966

I should explain, Mr. Speaker, that this bridge is going to replace one already existing approximately 65 feet from the site of the proposed bridge. From a procedural standpoint there is to be an agreement between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine which would cover the points arising in connection with the proposed construction, the ones I have just mentioned and such other questions as may arise.
In order to give this agreement its proper status there will be at an appropriate time an exchange of notes between the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) on behalf of Canada and representatives of the United States government in Ottawa, which will indicate the approval of the two federal governments to the conclusion of the agreement.
As I have stated, Mr. Speaker, I believe the bill is relatively straightforward, but I would be pleased to answer any questions from hon. gentlemen when we reach the committee stage.

Mr. Chairman, may I put two or three questions to the parliamentary secretary. The first is this. Has the government in mind any general bridge legislation? I believe it has been in contemplation for some time and it does seem to me that ought not to be necessary to come before this house each time an international bridge is to be constructed. It should be possible to set forth in general legislation the principles of
St. Croix River Bridge
management and the procedures of undertaking of these international works. I would appreciate it if the parliamentary secretary could tell the committee to what stage the government has gone in respect of this proposal.
The parliamentary secretary indicated that this bridge is to be toll free. I do not see any specific suggestion to that effect in the legislation except the use in line 13 of the words "for the free use and passage". Is that the only expression in the bill which makes it toll free?
Third, there is no provision in the bill that I am able to see, as I think there is, for example, in the Peace Bridge bill, for the management of the bridge. Is this to be a matter of equal right or equal representation of the two nations? By whom will the managers be appointed, the provincial authority in New Brunswick, the federal government, or by whom? The situation varies from international bridge to international bridge. We should have, I think, a clear understanding as to the authority that will appoint the body which is going to manage this particular bridge.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, the parliamentary secretary spoke of an agreement between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine. This is a matter which interests me. I should like him to explain in his capacity as parliamentary secretary by what technique such an agreement is reached as between a province and a state. Is this to be authorized by some action on the part of this parliament or have we some new technique whereby there is direct contact between a province and a state rather than it being an international affair conducted by the government of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. CROIX RIVER BRIDGE STRUCTURE TO CONNECT NEW BRUNSWICK AND MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I can deal with the hon. member's final question first because the answers to the other two questions which he has raised flow out of it. The procedure that was followed in this particular case was the following. As I mentioned on second reading, there is already in existence a bridge approximately 65 feet upstream from the proposed site, which bridge is operated under an existing agreement between the state of Maine and the province of New Brunswick.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
After some preliminary discussions were held between the province and the state of Maine with respect to replacing the existing

St. Croix River Bridge
bridge, the request was made by the government of New Brunswick to the government of Canada for authority to enter into more definitive arrangements with the state of Maine with respect to replacing the bridge. The government of Canada authorized the province of New Brunswick to enter into discussions with the state of Maine on several conditions. The first of these was that the draft agreement which it was proposed that the parties should enter into should be submitted first for the approval of the Department of External Affairs. Second, after the agreement was entered into and the appropriate legislation was passed by this house, a contemporaneous exchange of notes would take place between the two international persons, in this case the government of Canada and the government of the United States, whereby the international arrangement between the two countries would be consummated.
I might say that the draft agreement has in due course been submitted by the province of New Brunswick to the government of Canada, and after consideration the government of Canada has authorized the province of New Brunswick to enter into arrangements with the state of Maine in accordance with the terms of that agreement. Under the terms of that agreement it is stipulated that the bridge shall be toll free. Since it will be toll free the question which arose in connection with the Blue Water Bridge-and I think the hon. member mentioned the Peace Bridge at Niagara Falls-of establishing an international public authority to superintend operation and maintenance does not arise in this particular case.
The ownership of the bridge will rest in the entity on each side, in this case the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine, up to the international boundary. The operational costs will be taken care of in accordance with the terms of the agreement and paid on a pro rata basis by the two lesser governments. As I have said, this undertaking is in the agreement which has been approved by the government of Canada that it is to be toll free.
The hon. member raised the question whether this was a new departure or whether an agreement had been entered into between the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine whereby in some way the action of this parliament had been circumvented. speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Byrne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief statement to make which I hope will answer all possible questions in relation to this matter.
March 17, 1966

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company By Bill No. S-2 the National Capital Commission together with Canadian National Railway Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are endeavouring to implement the terms of an agreement made between them for the relocation of railways in the Ottawa area, dated October 17, 1963, which provides for the incorporation of a terminal railway company to consolidate and carry out rail terminal operations in the Ottawa area. This agreement was made not at the instigation of the railways but as a step in implementing the National Capital railway relocation plan.
I believe I can summarize in the interest of expedition. The bill was before the other place in 1965 when representations were made by those objecting to the wording, and again this session, the trucking companies objected to certain words which indicated that the railways might be taking over trucking in the Ottawa area. The bill has now been amended to make sure that the railway companies will only operate the normal pick-up and delivery services. There is an arrangement whereby both railway companies will share in the buildings and in the operation costs on a 50-50 basis.
A further objection was raised by railway employees who would be required to transfer to the new terminal railway company. This issue has been satisfactorily negotiated between the companies and the employees concerned so I believe I can now assure the house that all matters dealt with in the bill meet with the approval of all those who are concerned.

Mr. Speaker, the remarks made by the parliamentary secretary when introducing this bill may, as he suggested, have been all-embracing and sufficient to explain all the problems arising in connection with the measure before us. However, I doubt that this matter can really be settled so easily.
The house may recall that this bill was before us a year ago. The provisions of the measure do, indeed, give effect to its purpose but the method of doing so has caused severe dislocation of traffic in many areas and raises the whole question of the National Capital Commission plan in relation to railways and other transportation arteries throughout the area.
One of the problems presented by the bill is that it seeks to give legality to something which has already been done. The railway 
terminal we are talking about has already been developed and is due to be opened very shortly. There is in Ottawa at the present time, as will be seen from the newspapers, considerable discussion about whether or not a stay of execution can be granted for the present station in the downtown area because of its possible usefulness during the centenary year and because of the architecture of the building and the desire of some to retain it.
The fact that people will no longer be able to reach the central part of Ottawa by rail is a fait accompli. Any effort to change this situation is in my opinion bound to be ineffective. There is therefore no point in making a great issue of it. Nevertheless I think we should bear in mind when considering this bill that for many years we as members of parliament have had no opportunity to discuss with any thoroughness the affairs of the National Capital Commission and the relationship of the transportation system to the needs of this city and to the needs of the whole area within which the commission operates. The plan as set up by the National Capital Commission with the assistance of Mr. Greber many years ago has been modified, changed and discarded. This is only one, small example. It is proposed to set up now a company with capital stock of $30 million to be operated jointly by the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific Railways.
What does this really amount to? So far as passenger service is concerned there will be no operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway to be considered in relation to the terminal railway company. The only reason the C.P.R. is interested in this agreement is that there are one or two other joint terminal railway companies already established in various parts of Canada.
Since this bill was first presented circumstances have changed. The C.P.R. no longer provides passenger service between Toronto and Ottawa. It has only one train, the Canadian, coming into Ottawa. The indication given to the Board of Transport Commissioners is that the Canadian Pacific intends to ask for the discontinuation of all its passenger services in Canada. Should such a request be granted the company will no longer wish to operate a service in conjunction with anyone else. As I have pointed out, the situation in which the National Capital Commission is interested has changed and will change still more.
March 17, 1966

Some hon. members are aware that when the new station is completed there will no longer be a Hull railway terminal. The city of Hull will be without rail transportation when the provisions of this bill are fully implemented. I am surprised there are not more representatives of Ottawa and Hull here today because this is a matter which affects the people who live in these two cities. There are many agencies and groups in Ottawa and Hull who are very interested in the move to set up the Ottawa Terminal Railway Company because they know it will affect the whole railway passenger operation and the provision of passenger facilities. If the National Capital Commission is telling the house that this bill is a means of moving the railway out of the downtown section of Ottawa so that it can be located in a less congested part of the city, I suggest the commission is being unrealistic. In fact they have moved the railway lines only about four miles to the Alta Vista area which is growing rapidly. In the last five years the population in the Alta Vista area and the area adjacent to Industrial Avenue has doubled or trebled and possibly more.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
In my opinion, from the National Capital Commission's point of view there really is no plan in conjunction with the city of Ottawa to establish the type of development in this area that would be necessary to maintain a freight yard complex such as the Walkley terminal. In my view the National Capital Commission, for which we are responsible has really failed to do anything concrete in respect of the moving of the railway terminal. I am aware of the fact that the federal government really never has given consideration to what we are going to do with our national capital. How are we going to face this fact? I would think that some of the members, particularly those from this area, would be concerned about this matter.
You will be aware of the fact, Mr. Speaker, that one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard), the other night spoke of the potholes in the city of Ottawa and the fact that the National Capital Commission had not done much about it. I read a most idiotic statement in the press the other day made by Mr. Heit, a member of the board of control, to the effect that the member for Skeena should either shut up or put his money where his mouth is.
Ottawa Terminal Railway Company I am not sure whether he expects the hon. member for Skeena, who I think has property in this town, to finance the road building program himself. I do not know whether that is what he expects, but certainly the board of control in conjunction with the National Capital Commission really never has decided what it is going to do with the city. The situation is disgraceful in many respects so far as the public are concerned, and it is nothing to be proud of so far as the National Capital Commission is concerned. We are now compounding the problem by moving the railway terminal three miles from downtown Ottawa. Somebody has said that it only takes you a minute in your car to go downtown on the Queensway. That is true, but if you are riding on a train you have not brought your car in your pocket. I do not see what transportation by automobile has to do with railway transportation. If you travel by train you do not have your car with you, nor do you if you travel by airplane.
It is just as easy now to go by train from downtown Ottawa to downtown Montreal as it is to go from downtown Ottawa to Ottawa airport, fly to Dorval airport and then go from the airport to downtown Montreal. Do we have to be as stupid as the National Capital Commission? I do not know; maybe we do. I do not think anybody here is interested in this bill. I think we will pass it without hardly any comment. I am sure one or two of the Ottawa members will have to say something about it, but I really believe we do not care. I believe we have not given any consideration to this matter. We stupidly move the terminal three miles from downtown Ottawa and allow agencies of the government to put up our money for the building. The bill was not passed last year because the Liberal government did not have the guts to pass it when the committee added to the bill a provision that two members of the board of directors had to be French. This meant that the Canadian Pacific Railway had to be instructed that at least one of their directors would have to be a French Canadian. That was stupid. It has nothing to do with the bill or the National Capital Commission's decision in respect of where the terminal should go.
We went ahead and spent the money and built the building. It will be opened in a few months. We put it three miles from downtown and not in the heart of the industrial section. The street is called Industrial Avenue and has on it, I believe, Loeb's wholesale, a
March 17, 1968

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company couple of other small wholesalers and possibly a fruit provisioner, but who would call this the industrial part of Ottawa? I would be suprised if anyone would. We have moved the station three miles from downtown so that one has to hire transportation to get there when we already had the facilities downtown not two blocks from the parliament buildings and the main business section of the city. We did not think about the matter at all. We paid no more attention to the Ottawa terminal location than we paid to the moving of government facilities to Tunney's Pasture and to Confederation Heights, and to all the other stupid moves we allowed the National Capital Commission to make.
Members can pass this bill if they wish. They can modify it or do what they like with it. But I think the people who come after us are going to wonder about members of this parliament being so stupid that they did not ask the N.C.C. for a revision of the plan to bring it up to date. Mr. Greber probably is dead, if he is possibly he will turn over in his grave. The situation is a little like the matter of a house I built. The contractors looked at the plan I used and just did not believe it. Not knowing very much about plans, I modified them and in the end the plan I had bore no relation to the house I finally ended up building. As a result of modifying it here and there, it had no relationship to the plan the architect drew. I am sure Mr. Greber would feel this way about his plan in respect of the city of Ottawa and the whole greenbelt area. I am sure he would feel there is no relationship between his architectural design for the area and the plan we are now following. If .you doubt this, take a look at the plan and see the changes already in effect.
I am not sure what I can do, Mr. Speaker. I come from northern Ontario and this matter really does not concern me. However, I have an interest in seeing that the National Capital Commission as the national capital authority operates in a way of which the people of my area and every constituency in Canada can be proud. I expect there will be trains carrying passengers for some years and I do not like to see them having to arrive in Alta Vista. I should like to see them arrive downtown. When people come here from northern Ontario they are going downtown just as people are when they go to Montreal. If you go to New York city you do downtown. That should be kept in mind in developing new railway facilities. I agree that you do not 
have to take freight trains into the middle of town, but I think that passengers should be able to get off trains where normal transportation facilities are available at the door and where those who wish to walk will find themselves in the downtown part of the city.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have a responsibility. I am going to accept this responsibility and raise these matters again when the bill is referred to the committee. I think there is an obligation on the part of the house to send this bill to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I do not believe the sponsor of this bill said that he was going to do so. He shakes his head indicating he may not. Frankly, I think the law of the land says it has to go to a standing committee. That, of course, is not for me to decide. I suggest that even the discussion which took place last year indicated that the bill had no relationship to the plans which were developed for the area.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
Those from Ottawa who fought the last federal election will be aware of the fact that the Beachburg line is an important part of the Ottawa terminal railway system. It was and is a major concern of many people who live and are normally resident in Ottawa, including some members of parliament who make this city their permanent home. These people are very interested in this committee and should be given the opportunity of appearing before it to discuss this bill. If they are not given the opportunity I hope they will rise in righteous indignation and take to task some of those members of the Ottawa board of control who seem to have ffiends in this house who are willing to support the ideas and changes apparent in this proposal.
I do not think there is anything more I can usefully add. I believe every member will agree that it would be nice if we could save the Union Station but to do that we would probably have to cover a certain area of the canal in order that buildings, parks and gardens could be established above the cement tunnel through which the trains would travel.
I forget the estimated cost of this project which was given to the committee last year, but it was fairly small.
Surely all hon. members will agree that an open cut tunnel providing downtown facilities for the discharging and picking up of passengers would be a worth-while consideration. I
March 17, 1966	COMMONS
am sure the station could be rebuilt, modernized and used for other purposes such as a theatre, although for the life of me I cannot imagine why anyone would want a theatre in that area. That seems to be a pet project of some of the Ottawa board of control members.
If hon. members will think about this bill, surely they will realize that it is not a good one. We are providing the Canadian National with money through the back door to erect a building and adjoining facilities requiring a capitalization of some $30 million for which there has been no provision made yet. That is bad business in regard to any project. Any government that allows this to be done becomes the tail of a dog and it has no control over the wagging of that tail. It only provides the bones to feed the dog, the dog, of course, being the National Capital Commission which has been pushing parliament around for a long time.
The National Capital Commission is the child of parliament and it is the only body involved in the development of the national capital over which parliament has some control. For that reason we must have some say as to its actions. I think the bill now before us is in fact something we cannot change. To attempt to do so would be like trying to change during the consideration of the estimates amounts of money already spent by the government. The money has been paid, buildings have been erected and it is impossible to say afterwards that we are not going to erect those buildings or spend that money.
Perhaps it is my conservative attitude which encourages me to speak about this matter at all but I hope that hon. members, while realizing that the proposition before them is a fait accompli, will also realize that it does not meet the needs or wishes of the people living in the national capital who want a capital that is as beautiful as possible with facilities that will provide the services required for a national capital.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the provisions of this bill do not meet the requirements of the people of this area nor the general scheme of municipal development. I think it will be evident that others know more about the needs than I, but I am sure that every member who represents a constituency in the general area of Ottawa has received letters demanding that the city of Ottawa be established as a national capital city under the control of the federal government. That may not be in keeping with the wishes of the

Mr. Speaker, the strictures of the hon. member for Ti-miskaming (Mr. Peters) induce me to intervene very briefly in this debate. Most of the things he has said this afternoon he has said six, seven or eight years too late. He himself has conceded that the location of the railway station and lines in this community is a fait accompli. This afternoon he is simply threshing old straw because he knows he can get his name in the newspapers by this technique and create a considerable amount of publicity on the local Ottawa scene.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is very important to national capital planning. Without this bill it would be impossible to get rid of the many level crossings that exist in this community. It is a sine qua non to get rid of these level crossings.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member now addressing the house to address Your Honour rather than the hon. member for Timiskaming? He might as well be addressing me because I agree 100 per cent with the hon. member for Timiskaming.

Mr. Speaker, I thought I was addressing you but I submit it is quite legitimate to look to any section of the house at any particular time when speaking. I say, sir, that this bill, covering as it does the location of the central Union Station, is one in respect of which a decision was taken a considerable number of years ago. Whether or not that decison was wise at the time, it is now too late to do anything about it.
What the hon. gentleman has said this afternoon does point up a plea I have made on at least two occasions earlier this session to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), that all the plans and studies of the National Capital Commission should be referred to a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons for consideration. I do not suggest that the studies of such a committee would constitute an investigation of the commission at all. On the contrary, it would give the commission an opportunity to inform members of this house as to its basic plans and to indoctrinate them on the long range plans for the national capital.
March 17, 196$

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company
There is no use engaging now in harsh statements about what may have been done wrongly or otherwise in the past. It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to say that certain parts of this city are a disgrace and that we cannot be proud of them, but if there are problems in this city they are the result of long term neglect on the part of the parliament of Canada. The straightforward fact is that for many years the only contribution made by the parliament of Canada to the national capital was $100,000. That is why the neglect now shows and that is why it is taking so long to catch up. That is why there is an urgent need for a crash program for the centennial year.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The hon. gentleman mentioned one matter to which I think attention should be given and I hope the parliamentary secretary will make some reference to it when he speaks in closing the debate. I refer to the Beachburg line. My own view is that this particular bill has not gone far enough; it ought to go further, and the agreement ought to go further and provide for the abandonment of the Beachburg line. I am not going into that matter in any detail this afternoon but I shall be glad if the parliamentary secretary will indicate the stage and the nature of the studies which are now taking place in this connection. But I give him and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) notice that when the estimates of the Department of Public Works are before the house I intend to say considerably more on the subject of the Beachburg line and the fact that I believe that in the planning of the terminal and the attempts to abandon level crossings in this community we have not gone nearly far enough.
The hon. member for Timiskaming has put forward many strictures against the National Capital Commission. I believe that the staff and the members of the commission are dedicated people. Frequently I have criticized them and frequently I shall criticize them in the house, but I think the opportunity should be given to them to come before a committee of the house and there expose the long range plans so that we will not be confronted with the situation with which we are confronted this afternoon wherein the hon. gentleman six, seven or eight years too late, raises the subjects that he has raised. If we had before a committee of this house the opportunity to study the long range plans, we would be sure

there would be parliamentary approval, parliamentary sanction and parliamentary backing for this national capital as the true symbol of a united nation.

Mr. Speaker, could I ask the parliamentary secretary a question? I was on the transport committee in the last parliament. I am not on it this year. I do not need to ask why. I am surprised to find that there are so many of my French speaking compatriots who have so low an opinion of the dignity of their racial origin that they are prepared to be fobbed off with this sort of an arrangement. There are countries where this procedure is followed which do not stand very high in the estimation of other people throughout the world. I have only to call your attention, sir, to the Republic of South Africa where a minority is fobbed off with one or two seats in the house of parliament and they are supposed to be satisfied with that situation.
I suggest to my French speaking friends that they should not be satisfied with such a proposal. If there are ten French speaking Canadians who are best suited for this job there should be ten French speaking Canadians on the board of directors. It is a shocking thing to me that French Canadian

Ottawa Terminal Railway Company people, with a proud record and proud ancestry, are prepared to pay so little heed to the respect of their own people.

Mr. Chairman, to my mind, the member who has just resumed his seat, spoke unfortunate words. There was confusion at the outset with regard to the very subject of the amendment. The amendment does not ask that there be two French Canadians on the board of directors.
This amendment is not, therefore, of a racial nature. It asks that at least two directors speak French. They may be of other origins than French, but at least we recognize the principle of bilingualism in legislative measures and this, to me, is important.
If we do not err at the start, I think we can eventually manage to reach an understanding. I expect, Mr. Chairman, that if you were to read the amendment again, the hon. members would see what this is all about.

May I ask that the amendment be read, please?
Would the minister permit a question? Did the minister not hear the French speaking member refer continually in his speech to French Canadians?

I heard, indeed; only, I am limiting myself to the terms of the amendment for that is what will be incorporated into the act, and the amendment we are discussing is intended to confirm the question of bilingualism.
The amendment asks-let us stick to the amendment-that two members be appointed who speak French. I do not think that under those circumstances we are dealing with a racial matter. We are merely confirming bilingualism in Canada. If you confirm it through law, as experience has already proved, we will achieve that goal.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after hearing you read the amendment, I entirely agree with the Associate Minister of Defence (Mr. Cadieux). We do not want the matter to develop into a racial issue, at all, but it is time perhaps to give a concrete example in order that bilinguism be recognized in our statutes.
It is possible that the persons appointed to this board of directors will not be French Canadians, but French speaking, and on that basis, I am willing to vote for the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that under the pretext of non-discrimination, discrimination will be sanctioned instead in a statute.
If I understand correctly, Canada is rapidly evolving at present toward the recognition of two majority groups, toward a bilingual, an entirely bilingual, country.
It is to place ourselves in an inferior position to suggest, by passing this amendment, that only two persons will have to be French speaking out of five, seven or ten-
At least two.
At least two.

It is to admit that five, seven or eight persons out of ten could be unilingual.
I feel then that we should provide instead that all of them should be bilingual, and tend toward this policy.
I think this is exactly the opposite of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) the other day, when he said that the fact of being bilingual does not add anything to a person's competence, because it could simply happen by accident.
In my opinion, to insert this amendment in a statute is to go in the opposite direction and we suggest by the same token that it must imposed to a minority group in our country, when we know that it is the minority which is bilingual. And when it is wished to make the country completely bilingual, especially the higher officials.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), and his statements on the specific and current question seem rather strange.
I think that the Minister, being a newcomer to the house, may not be aware of all the complexities surrounding the institution of this Ottawa Terminal Railway company.

This bill was before the transport committee last year, Mr. Chairman, and questions were put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and to the parliamentary secretary who represented him. At the time, I think it was the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Cantin) who was parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport.
He was asked whether the directors of the company had been approached. The present parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Byrne) does not know but last year it was confirmed in the parliamentary committee on transport that the directors of this company who were to be appointed had been approached by the Minister and that none of them spoke French. Such was the answer we had at the time.
That is why last year, when the bill came before the committee, an amendment was moved that at least two of the directors should be French speaking. Why? Because the parliamentary secretary admitted before the committee that no one speaking French was among those appointed.
In other words, we were in precisely the same situation as that described by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
When it becomes obvious that there are no French Canadian directors, then we will resort to other means including the law. Well, that is what came out last year, that the future directors had been approached and that not one of them was French speaking.
When, last year, by a vote of 14 to 11-if my memory serves me right-the committee felt that it was appropriate to amend the bill so that at least two directors would be French speaking, that was for the specific case of the company which was to administer the railway station here, in Ottawa. It was precisely for that purpose because the facts had shown that there was not a single French speaking director.
In view of the facts, and since the directors have been approached and not one of them is French speaking, there is only one thing left for us to do as legislators and that is to use the law to force the minister's hand. If he acted too quickly in his search for directors for his company, he only has to retreat, to change his mind and to take steps to have at least two French speaking persons appointed.
As things stand now. there is only one recourse open to us and that is to impose them under the law. I do not contend that such an amendment must be introduced in all cases. I am saying no such thing but that is 23033-179
Ottawa Terminal Railway Company what should be done in this specific case. Last year, in the committee, we were told that all the directors had been approached and that not one of them was French speaking, but the committee decided to suggest an amendment. This year, the government comes back with the same bill but without the amendment.
What are they trying to hide? Have promises been made to certain individuals who have served the party well? What is it? Are friends involved? I know that is not the point. I should like to know why the Minister of Transport is proposing the same bill for the second year, but after having taken off an amendment which was inserted last year by transport committee.
I remember quite well that the one-I think it was Douglas Fisher, the former member for-

Now, the minister is coming back with the same bill, but he has deleted the amendment. Under the present circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I think that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration must review his position and understand that we are not dealing with a general case but with a specific case, where they want to force directors upon us, even before the company is formed and before the bill is passed. So I think that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration must review his position and change his attitude now that he is acquainted with the facts.

Mr. Chairman, there are only two points I wish to discuss. There is surely some confusion in the minds of those who took part in the debate and maybe even in the mind of the man who is now speaking. Therefore, in any case, I think that, since we want to protect bilingualism, if the amendment said that there must be on the committee or commission two people who can understand and speak French fluently, that is in accordance with the spirit of bilingualism.
But if we talk about French speaking Canadians, there is here a connotation which concerns the French Canadians as an ethnic group. It is a way of designating the French Canadians. That is where I disagree. I do not accept that the ethnic group to which I belong should need a legal text to protect itself. I am just saying to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) and to the house, and even to the public, that if tomorrow the commission concerned is created and if the biethnic character of Canada is not taken into account, I will join him to make representations. We will fight together about the same thing, irrespective of party discipline. That matter means a lot to me.
However, I do not think that we should fight in the name of the act. Besides, the hon. member for Lapointe should be the last one to want to hang on to means which, in my opinion, are used by groups which recognize their inferiority at the outset.
He knows himself that when he brought up the question of the C.N.R., his intervention was much stronger than if he had only called upon the act. He knows it very well and that is what we must do and not try to say: We need to be protected in a special way in legislation just as it is done in some associations to protect women.
That is what I wanted to say and my remarks must not be misunderstood. I know that, politically, I am on dangerous ground -but it is not the first time-and that what I said can be misinterpreted. As far as the goal is concerned, I am completely in agreement. I am just saying that I do not accept, in principle, a means like the one suggested and I will gladly do some picketing with the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) and the hon. member for Lapointe if ever the representation is not made on a fair basis.

I, for one, always wondered-this may seem somewhat original-but I always asked myself the question, and I was even waiting for the report of the Royal Commission on bilingualism and biculturalism for enlightenment on this matter, what is a French speaking Canadian? Mr. Chairman, I have a few words to say about this resolution. I know that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) is aware of the problem I shall mention. I have referred to it many times in the house. It is an important problem to be solved.
Mr. Chairman, the government is about to increase the number of members of the Northwest Territories Council and to extend their responsibilities and jurisdiction. This is the first step towards the creation of another Canadian province, the Northwest Territories. The same will apply to Yukon and this is where I object. This raises a problem that should be solved without delay.
The Northwest Territories also comprise a whole series of islands around the province of Quebec, situated less than 12 miles from the shore line at low tide. A whole series of uninhabited islands. Being less than 12 miles from the Quebec coast, they are at the same time hundreds of miles away from the rest of the Northwest Territories. The day the Northwest Territories becomes a province, these islands will be 300 or 400 miles from the rest of the Northwest Territories while almost within the territory of the province of Quebec.
At the present time, they are considered as part of the Northwest Territories and seem practically linked to Quebec by land, in spite of which they are included in the Northwest Territories.
Well, I suggest that those islands will create a grave problem for Canada before long, especially when the Northwest Territories are divided into provinces, as this is bound to happen sooner or later.
So we have a problem there. It is geographically abnormal and illogical to include in the Territories islands that are practically tied together but located three or four hundred miles away and this is paving the way for a dispute between two provinces, the province of the Northwest Territories and the province of Quebec. The Canadian government will be the one to be hit on the rebound.
DEBATES	2839
Northwest Territories Act
Now is the time-and I am saying this to the minister-while all those islands are uninhabited, when there is no trade, no industry, nothing there, to hand them over to Quebec, as all geographers and map makers in Canada have recommended.
Indeed, they have recommended that all islands which at low tide are located within those twelve miles be included in the territory of the province of Quebec. You will also note that those islands are uninhabited at present. Today, that could be done quite easily. If the minister remembers-I think that at the time his parliamentary secretary was the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner), who answered questions on behalf of the minister at the committee meetings- to the representatives of the Northwest Territories who, for two or three years, came before that committee to look after the interests of the Northwest population before the committee-I think it was the committee on mines, forests and waters-I asked the following question:
Would you object to the federal government taking over all the islands within twelve miles at low tide around the province of Quebec and giving them to the province of Quebec? No one objected to it. On the contrary, they were unanimous to say: "We do not need them; they are situated at many hundreds of miles from the rest of the territory and if ever the administration were forced to look after those islands, that would be very complicated for the rest of the Northwest Territories."
The people of the Northwest Territories themselves would be quite willing to get rid of these islands by giving them to the province of Quebec.
Well, Mr. Chairman, when these islands are uninhabited, when the representatives of the Northwest Territories are willing to leave all those islands to the province of Quebec, when all this could be done without anyone objecting, I submit the minister should decide to hand over these islands to the province of Quebec.
He just has to consult geographers and map-makers and he will realize that at the present time, this is an abnormal and illogical situation from a geographical viewpoint. It is absolutely abnormal. All the shores at low tide supposedly belong to the Northwest Territories. However, if a citizen of the province of Quebec decided to build a cottage along the shores of the Hudson Bay, and to

Northwest Territories Act add a wharf, well, just because the wharf would come in the water at low tide, this would be under federal jurisdiction. The shores come under the federal government, although such is not the case for other shores on inland waters.
Well, Mr. Chairman, I think the minister should decide that those islands belong to Quebec and the time has come to do so.
I urge the minister to take the opportunity of this legislation and include in the bill a clause stipulating that all the islands situated within twelve miles from the shore at low tide be given to Quebec.
I think all hon. members should support such a resolution. This would be a proof of wisdom and foresight. In fact, this would prevent conflicts which this situation might stir up later. I urge the minister to take this into consideration. The minister knows that I have been raising this problem in the House for two or three years. Besides, the time has gone by where the Eskimos were considered here as second-rate citizens, because we did not have the facilities to enable them to enjoy our standard of living and to offer them an education to which they were entitled.

I have made the statement that in the long run I think it would be better for the people who reside there to have a greater degree of control over their own affairs, even if they make errors. I want to reply to the hon. member for Lapointe, who brought up a point which has been before the house on earlier occasions. He referred to the boundaries of the provinces. I would remind him that this bill does not confirm or amend the boundaries of the provinces. The hon. member is referring in substance to that myriad of granite fingers which point themselves out of the sea all around the northern coasts of Quebec. But not all are pure granite, as he knows; there are two or three extremely valuable islands there upon which there are considerable mineral resources, particularly iron.
I know the hon. member will not wish to hold up the progress of the extension of a greater degree of self-determination to the people who live in the Territories in order to press for an amendment to the boundaries of the provinces. I do not know by what measure the boundaries of the provinces could be adjusted, but certainly not by a measure such as we are discussing at this resolution stage tonight.
The fact of the matter is that all of those islands in the Hudson Bay, indeed those islands in James Bay too, are not part of the provinces of either Ontario or Quebec, but are part of the Northwest Territories. I have said before that the time may well come when they will be allotted to the provinces, but that is certainly not within the compass of the bill under discussion tonight.
Finally I want to thank the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres for his very thoughtful suggestion. I would remind him in this connection-I had thought some other hon. members in the house would raise the matter-that at the present time a royal commission in the Northwest Territories under the chairmanship of Professor Carrothers is taking a survey of what might be the future of government in the Northwest Territories. It is a very excellent commission. They made the rounds of a number of communities in the summertime and they are now doing the same thing in the depths of winter. The evidence they are getting I have no knowledge of, but from what I read in the papers it is obvious that there is a very healthy ferment in the Northwest Territories which indicates that people are thinking in terms of their future and their ambitions.
Some provinces are proposing that their boundaries be extended to take over the section of the Northwest Territories to their north. However, at this stage I do not think we should prejudge anything. I hope we may

Mr. Chairman, I must say I am not at all pleased with the Minister's reply. He said: "I do not know how to go about setting the limits or boundaries of the provinces."
Well, Mr. Chairman, if he does not know how to do it, let him resign. He is supposed to solve problems. It is not enough to say: "I do not know how to go about it." Let him find out. Together with his officials and his deputy minister, he should find the answer. He asks us not to hold up the adoption of a bill, but he knows that two years ago a bill was held up in committee because it was felt that the "jurisdiction" of the Northwest Territories should not be increased until such time as problems like this were not settled.
This problem must be solved, while the federal government still has the authority to do so; for, when the Northwest Territories have greater "jurisdiction", powers and privileges to govern themselves, then, it will be too late.
It seems to me the minister should have a greater sense of responsibility. He knows that the situation is not normal, that it will be a source of useless bickering and struggles, because the federal government can at present settle the matter. Within ten or fifteen years, maybe sooner, it will have to be settled between the two provinces.
Privileges and powers are being given the Northwest Territories, but once they have them, the federal government will no longer be able to solve the problem of the islands.
It must be settled now. The minister says: Allow the legislation to be passed. We do not know what to do about that but let the IMr. Lalng.]
legislation pass so that its benefits are not delayed.
But if disadvantages are to follow also, should we ignore them?
The minister is wondering if that can be included in such a legislation. Of course that can be the subject of an amendment to the bill that is put before us by the minister.
The minister introduces a bill to give responsibilities to the Northwest Territories. But by giving them such responsibilities he should solve the problems that exist, namely about borders.
It seems to me that it would be easy for the minister to prepare an amendment or a supplementary section to the effect that all the islands located 12 miles from the territory of the province of Quebec, at low tide, belong to that province. That is simple enough and, I repeat, particularly since the minister knows, because he was told when I questioned the representatives from the Northwest Territories, that none of them objected to that proposal. On the contrary, at the present time, they do not know what to do with those uninhabited islands which are located several hundred miles from the Northwest Territories and only a few miles from the province of Quebec.
When the Northwest Territories are made into a province, including the little islands which are located near the borders of Quebec, what will the minister be able to do when the time comes to settle the matter of borders between the two provinces?
If one stands on the shore of Hudson's bay, at high tide, one is said to be on the mainland, in the province of Quebec. On the other hand, at low tide, on the shore, one is in the Northwest Territories. Therefore, when the Northwest Territories become a province, one will have to go to another province for a swim. That does not make sense and the minister knows it.
What would it be for him to add a section which would give privileges or extend the jurisdiction of the citizens of the Northwest Territories and, at the same time, include an other section to settle that problem once and for all by saying: All these islands which lie within 12 miles of the Quebec shores, at low tide, belong to the province of Quebec.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to pursue the subject upon which we have embarked in the last few moments because it is one that concerns most of the provinces in this country of ours. I can remember, for example, back in the early 1950's sitting in on a conference in northern Manitoba where it was suggested that most of the Northwest Territories be joined to the northern part of the provinces, and a new territory be carved out, to be called Precambria, which I think
2844	COMMONS DEBATES	March 17, 1966
Northwest Territories Act was the name designated at that time. Sir, if we were to embark on a discussion of this kind at the present time, I am sure we should be spending many hours in debate. I agree with the minister that this is something that will have to be considered at some time, but in the proper context and under the proper circumstances.
My reason for rising again is to correct an historical reference made by the minister in regard to the construction of the Pine Point Railway. I know he did not intend to state it in these terms, but I believe he did quote the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition as having referred to two rusted lines into the territory. For the sake of the record I should like to point out to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources that the Header of the Opposition was merely quoting the immortal words of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who led when he was in opposition a concerted attack in this house, against the whole idea of the construction of a railway into the Northwest Territories. To climax his argument, he wrote the whole thing off as a situation which would result in a railway line that would eventually disappear because of rust resulting from lack of use.
If our estimate with respect to 225,000 tons of ore per year from the Pine Point mine was what might be called a conservative estimate as a potential in the initial stages, I think the minister will agree that our attitude and our approach to the prospects of economic development in the Territories was much more liberal than that represented by the words of the gentleman who was rewarded for his particularly visionary contribution to the future of transportation in Canada by being made Canadian Minister of Transport under the Liberal administration.
For the sake of the historic accuracy I should also point out that the 225,000 ton figure was reached as a result of negotiations with the representatives of Cominco. speakerposition: Minister of Industry; Minister of Defence Production
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT AND DEFINITION OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in every enlightened nation there has developed, within recent years, an awareness of the impact of science and technology upon every facet of life; an influence that is reflected in the economic growth, the health and well being of peoples, the physical comforts, the release
IMr. Laing.]
from drudgery, the provision of time to practise and enjoy the arts, indeed in the entire social fabric not the least component of which is the political relations within and between nations. Equally well recognized is the implication that if science, in its many ramifications, is to serve the community and the nation to best advantage there must be some rationale, some orderly progress, some planning that takes into consideration the needs, the aspirations, the resources, the capabilities-yes, even the conscience of a people. For science must serve-not control-not only the greatest possible number of individuals, nor only one nation, but the great international community of man.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
In many countries, Great Britain, Sweden, Germany, the United States, France, Japan, to name but a few, the serious need for long term planning in science and technology has been recognized for a number of years and appropriate action has been taken by the governments concerned to establish organizations charged with the duty of obtaining competent expert opinion on scientific and technological matters and providing governments with recommendations and advice upon which policy decisions can be based. As may be expected, the character of the organization is not the same in all countries but varies with the size, complexity and political philosophy of the individual nation. All, however, have developed formal organizations concerned with advising the government on the formulation of scientific policy.
It will be recalled that the Glassco Commission, in examining the situation in Canada, found that the mechanism by which objective and independent recommendations in respect of scientific policy could be brought before the government was not functioning. The commission proposed, therefore, that there should be established an advisory committee composed of people knowledgeable in science and its applications, which would have the responsibility of examining the several facets of science in Canada and of making recommendations to government upon which policy could be formulated. The commission emphasized that the advisory body should be independent and not directly associated with any operating agency.
As the house was informed by the Prime Minister on April 30, 1964, the recommendations of the Glassco Commission were studied by Dr. C. J. Mackenzie, a former President of the National Research Council, and following

for
March 17, 1966

his recommendation the government later that year established the science secretariat in the office of the Privy Council. Dr. Mackenzie noted at the time that before an advisory committee could be brought into being the role of the National Research Council should be re-examined and its position in relation to the proposed advisory committee defined.
Based on studies made in consultation with the National Research Council and other interested parties it has been decided to establish an advisory body to be known as the Science Council of Canada to advise the government on matters concerning broad national scientific policy. This decision takes account of the interests and functions of government departments and agencies whose activities are related to science and technology. Lest there be some misunderstanding of the term "science" in the name of the proposed council, it should be clearly stated that in this context it includes all the natural sciences over the broad spectrum from "pure" science to "applied" science, from the search for new scientific knowledge to its application in the service of man in such fields as engineering, medicine, agriculture and industry.
The purpose of the Science Council will primarily be to define and determine feasible long term objectives for science in Canada, to suggest appropriate paths for reaching them and to consider the responsibilities of the various segments of the industrial, academic and government communities in this field. The Council will be less concerned with day to day problems than with developing principles and evolving a philosophy upon which future courses can be charted. Other countries have experienced very rapid growth in science and science-based enterprises during the past five to ten years. In some cases the possible effects of growth were not anticipated or recognized, with the result that there developed an imbalance in the size of government agencies involved, in the disciplines supported and in the geographic distribution of scientific and industrial activity that, because of its magnitude, is now difficult if not impossible to correct. In Canada, although we have made notable advances in some areas, there is every indication that the next ten years will see a particularly rapid growth period in science and technology, especially perhaps in industry, and in the

Science Council of Canada universities which must produce the manpower for the envisaged expansion of all science.
A particularly difficult and complex problem in the modern age is to determine the priority that should be accorded to the growth of a particular branch of science or technology at a given time for the optimum benefit of the country. It is obvious that Canada, with its limited means, cannot afford full support to all areas of science and consequently we must, during the period of rapid growth that lies immediately ahead, utilize our physical and human resources to the best advantage by exercising a degree of selection and making a resolute effort to determine the areas upon which support should be concentrated, while at the same time availing ourselves of the experience of other countries. It is our hope that the Science Council will undertake to develop basic concepts which will serve as guides for the allocation of these resources.
In this respect the Council will provide advice to the government upon which policy in respect of science and technology can be established. It will be the duty of the Council to assess in a comprehensive manner Canada's scientific and technological resources, requirements and potentialities and to make recommendations thereon to the minister. The Council will be advisory only and will have no direct authority over expenditures or budgets of any government department or agency.
Whatever policies may be adopted for the future of science in Canada, one thing is certain, that unless there is a sufficient number of well trained, intelligent and enterprising personnel skilled in the exploration and application of science the desired objectives will not be achieved. The effective development and utilization of scientific and technological manpower will be a primary concern of the Council.
As science is but one of the several components of modern society that together determine the course of human affairs, any studies that are made to determine the role and the objectives of science must inevitably take into account the possible effects on the society in which we live. Matters such as public health, employment patterns, the safety and survival of communities, the enjoyment of liesure and of old age, the philosophy of culture and of law, the entire fabric of the economy and many others can be profoundly affected by scientific and technological change
March 17, 1966

Science Council oj Canada whether internal or international. The Science Council in delineating feasible objectives will be expected to consult and collaborate with other agencies and organizations in different fields to ensure that fullest consideration is given to the correlation of its objectives with the broad spectrum of social needs.
Science, in its many ramifications, has within it the potential to serve not only individuals but communities and the entire nation by providing better living, new employment opportunities, easier communication and countless other social and economic advantages. But the complex problem of determining the attainable objectives and of defining the role that science and technology can play will require for its solution the serious attention of enlightened, intelligent and public-spirited people who are aware of the implications of science in our economy and our society. We earnestly believe that the Science Council of Canada as it is now proposed will provide a particularly effective means of obtaining factual information and thoughtful opinions and of correlating them to form a most suitable background for the formulation and construction of government policy.
