Mr. Chairman, in rising to support the resolution the minister has just put forward in the name of the government, let me just say that we on this side of the house really feel that the government and all parliamentarians have a real and active role to play in encouraging what we recognize as individual and national excellence. I think that if we support the resolution the minister has put forward in a real and tangible way, we will have moved at least one step forward in encouraging in this nation individual and national excellence. To my mind individual and national excellence means one thing, that as legislators we should expect nothing but the best from our nation and each and every citizen in our country which we call Canada.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Tonight I think I speak for all members on this side of the house when I say that while we recognize there is much yet to be done we should be very proud of the role which the National Research Council in this country has played in the past. I think the minister will agree that this is a Council of which Canadians should be very proud. We should also be proud of the role that our scientists have played in general, apart from the role 
the National Research Council has played in particular.
In my brief remarks this evening I should like to touch on an idea mentioned by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the House of Commons a few nights ago. We in Canada living north of the United States of America, a country which has the highest standard of economic living in the world, are in a particular vulnerable position. It seems to me that in attempting in an economic sense to keep up with the Jones, we invariably enter into areas of activity into which we in fact have no business to go. The facts of everyday life dictate that living north of the United States we in Canada are obliged both at home and abroad to enter into various fields of activity, economically, politically and, if you will, socially.
However, too often we pay attention to the bigness of our ventures rather than the quality of our enterprises, and it is for this reason I am most interested in the fact that in his very good speech this evening the minister used the word "selection". This will be one of the jobs of this council.
I believe that rather than paying attention to the bigness of our ventures we should base our national activities on the idea of individual and national excellence, and we should moreover underline specialization and selectivity. Specialization and selectivity should keynote our national approach to economic ventures. I am very glad the minister mentioned the word "selection" tonight because it does fit in with the general remarks I have to make.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, we should support the idea of individual and national excellence, and we should go on to support the resolution, the work of the National Research Council and the endeavours of this new body which the minister is setting up, as well as the endeavours of Canadian scientists.
The minister has very ably said this evening that in a country like Canada, which has vast resources but a small population spread out from Atlantic to Pacific, we must select the areas of scientific activity which we are going to support. But this is a very difficult thing to do. Because of this fact it is impossible for us to give the kind of support to all the scientific endeavours which we should like to give at the present time.
However, with this in view, I would put before the house the suggestion that as a country up until now we have not allowed-I
March 17. 1966	COMMONS
do not blame any government entirely tor this-sufficient importance to be placed on the support of scientific research in Canada. It is my belief that the government and the country that does not support adequately enough scientific research is merely killing the goose that lays the golden egg. For every dollar spent to assist a scientist in Canada, the United Kingdom spends $5 and the United States government $10 to $15.
In my short remarks this evening on this resolution, while I am not going to enter into a debate on this question, I realize it is of very great concern to the minister that this country is faced with a scientific brain drain. We have listened to both sides of the question, and I will be the first to admit to the government that it is a very difficult problem to discuss and resolve especially this evening. But I think that on balance this country is faced with a brain drain of scientists who are seeking employment outside of Canada. It is not an easy problem to solve, but I suggest that support of this resolution would help the minister to find a solution to this problem which is presently facing the nation.
I hope I will not be out of order if I refer to another reserach council which falls under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Industry. I am referring to medical research, a matter which I hope will receive priority. The other night I mentioned in the house that in my view, Canada is facing a very serious shortage of doctors. Approximately the same number of medical graduates graduated from our medical schools last year as were leaving ten years ago. Yet, some 400 of the 1,000 medical graduates who graduated from our universities last year left the country. At the same time hundreds of qualified students are being turned away from our medical schools. Why? The reason is we lack teachers.
Why do we lack teachers in our medical schools? And I am told that if we are going to have enough teachers by 1970, excluding all considerations relating to medicare, we will need 2,000 medical teachers for our medical schools. At the moment we have only 1,000. In the United States last year, 90 per cent of the assistance given to scientific research in medical schools originated from the federal government and amounted to approximately $1,300 million.
Contrast this with the state of affairs in Canada, where governmental assistance amounted to about $15 million. I am not blaming the government for this. There has been a long tradition of inadequate assistance

It is pretty difficult to visualize just what will be the eventual role and function of this Science Council, beyond noting what was said by the minister in his opening remarks on the resolution. Certainly, in so far as this measure goes it receives the support, I am sure of almost all members because there is a crying need in this country for expanded science research facilities and capabilities, if we are to be able to say that we are doing our best to improve our industrial productivity, economic efficiency and so on.
The second annual report of the Economic Council of Canada makes it pretty clear, Mr. Chairman, that the industrial development of our country depends directly on the quality and quantity of our institutions of education and scientific research.
March 17, 1966

Science Council of Canada
Through the provincial governments of this country we have been accelerating our efforts in education. However, I am not so sure about the scientific research aspect, and our responsibilities toward that aspect in the 1960's, because I have gained the impression from the few journals I have read that Canada is somehow lagging behind other countries in the expansion of science research institutions and facilities.
If we are really concerned, as I believe we are, about our industrial productivity-and this is the term we hear so often in this house and across the country-and if we are really concerned about our competitiveness in the export markets of the world; if we are really concerned about the adequacy of our scientific and industrial research capability, and if we are really concerned about the so-called brain drain, which is another term we hear so much about, the federal government must lead the way in expanding the size and scope of our post graduate institutions in their role as centres of scientific research.
Mr. Chairman, what I am trying to say is that scientific research should not be regarded, as it seems to have been regarded up to now, as something almost exclusively under the jurisdiction of the provinces. This whole matter is related to education. I suggest that the time is ripe for the federal government to assert a greater degree of leadership in helping to expand scientific research facilities in Canada.
I believe there are several compelling reasons why the federal government should be taking the lead, and I do not think that the establishment of an advisory council type of project is adequate to the task that lies ahead.
What are some of these obvious reasons to which I have alluded? What are some of these obvious reasons why the federal government should undertake greater responsibility in this field? One reason, Mr. Chairman, is obvious. It is that scientific research is a costly proposition. Therefore attempts should be made to avoid duplication and overlapping as between the different universities under different provincial jurisdictions. Another reason is that if there were greater federal leadership, if there were federal coordination, specialization in scientific research could be effected. There must be specialization as between the different institutions that go in for science research. It seems to me that we have to attempt to obtain the economy of 
scale and the economy that comes with specialization in research. This can be achieved to a much greater degree if there is federal leadership.
I would put forward yet a third reason, Mr. Chairman. That is, that our industrial productivity and export positions are matters relating to our entire Canadian economy. It follows therefore that industrial or applied science research, as it is sometimes called, must be national-economy oriented. However, industrial research or applied science research in turn is dependant upon the research that is carried on in our postgraduate science faculties, because it depends for its personnel on the academic centres, especially on the universities. Those academic centres must turn out, and must graduate scientists. Some of those will stay in the academic community. Some of them obviously would then be available for our industrial research centres.
Canada has not been doing very well at all so far, Mr. Chairman. The previous speaker made some references to scientific research performance in Canada, as compared with that in the United States and Great Britain. One reason why we have not been doing too well in this country is that many of our people upon graduation leave for the United States. There is greater opportunity in the United States for them. It is contended by some people that this so-called brain drain is somehow counterbalanced by the immigration into Canada of scientists from Europe, and particularly from Great Britain.
I would submit that the scientists and personnel that we do get from the old country are, for the most part, at a lower level of achievement in their careers than those leaving Canada for the United States. Men holding degrees at the doctorate level leave Canada for the United States. People at the bachelor level in science emigrate to Canada from the old country. Canada is losing all the while. This has to do with lack of opportunity here.
In the minute or two left before ten o'clock I should like to take an opportunity to quote some sentences from a letter written by a science graduate of Canada to the editor of the journal Physics in Canada. I quote:
Dear Sir:
In the near future I will be faced with the prospect of being forced to desert Canada (which will have "invested" over ten thousand dollars in my education) for the brighter research opportunities in the United States.
March 17, 1966	COMMONS
Unfortunately Canada's political elements seem to be unaware of the seriousness of the situation. I therefore suggest that it would do far more good to send this and similar articles directly to individual Members of Parliament-
-pointing out the problem.
For obvious reasons, Mr. Chairman, I need not name the writer.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.

IMMIGRATION-INQUIRY AS TO STATEMENT ON SEDGWICK REPORT
speechtext:
This afternoon I asked the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration a question about the Sedgwick report on immigration he tabled a few days ago. I am glad to take this opportunity to expand my question.
Mr. Sedgwick is an eminent lawyer. Whether he has any experience in immigration matters I do not know. His report contained some good suggestions, but there are other recommendations which cause great anxiety and I would urge the minister to repudiate them promptly. I refer to the recommendations in the report that sponsorship of immigrants be limited to spouses and minor children.
Members of this house will know that in recent years there have been two main streams of immigration. The first group has been selected on the basis of special skills and qualifications and has been based directly on economic motives. The second group has been admitted on social, family and humanitarian grounds. The basis of selection here has been on the ground of relationship to Canadian citizens and residents.
In his report Mr. Sedgwick makes a derogatory reference to large numbers of what he calls unskilled and functionally illiterate adults who have come to Canada through the sponsorship movement. If he were more aware of the facts he would know that a very large number of these sponsored immigrants have become established in a whole series of useful occupations and have made a useful contribution to this country.
The admission of unskilled immigrants to Canada in the past was due to deliberate
DEBATES	2853
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion government policy of selection, when it was thought advisable to seek unskilled labour to do some of the jobs Canadians did not care to do. I protest that Mr. Sedgwick's suggestion would practically eliminate considerations of family obligation and humanity, from our immigration policy.
In my view an attempt to base our immigration policy solely on economic considerations and to eliminate family and humanitarian considerations would be unworthy of Canada. It would, for example, prevent sons or daughters bringing their aged parents to this country, though they might well be in a position to do so. It would prevent the possibility of a successful immigrant bringing over his children, if they were over 21, or his grandparents, or orphaned children from Hong Kong-a case I have in mind.
The whole trouble is that Mr. Sedgwick maintains a restrictionist mentality. He keeps on saying that no alien has a right to come to Canada. He ignores the clear intention of parliament, as expressed in the present act, to give a limited statutory right to persons who are qualified and who do not fall within the prohibitions in the act or in the regulations. He apparently does not know that this has been pronounced by the Chief Justice of Canada who specifically referred, in one particular case, to the statutory right to bring qualified persons to Canada.
I hope the minister will give us an assurance that the government has no intention of preventing Canadian citizens who have the means to do so from bringing close relatives to Canada other than husbands, wives and minor children. If he gives this undertaking he will relieve a great deal of anxiety, for there are many people in Canada who look forward to bringing members of their family here when the time comes to do so. I hope the minister will use his good judgment in accepting the good parts of the report and rejecting the bad parts, which include the basic philosophy that parliament has given no rights in the field of immigration.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, a generous humanitarian immigration policy is not only in accordance with humanity but is also in Canada's own best interests. I hope the minister will be able to give us assurances on this matter.

The point he raised is extremely important. I know to what extent it can affect a great number of Canadians. It is a point we shall consider very earnestly and closely. Unfortunately, I cannot give him the assurance he is asking for tonight without prejudice to the cabinet's decision. I do not think I should give any further reasons. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) understands very well that in the house, outside the cabinet, I cannot commit myself on behalf of the government.
We have based ourselves on two criteria: professional skills and qualifications, and the second one, sponsorship, that is, by the immigrant in Canada who, according to our statutes, was entitled to send for his relatives. I believe that the second point, namely, sponsorship, should remain one of the basic criteria of our immigration to Canada.
We are not accepting machines, they are men with problems, men with relatives. In short, this might seem a bit ridiculous, but if Canada needs an engineer and finds one in Germany, if the latter finds out after getting here that he is unable to send for his mother whom he was supporting back in Germany-some provisions may seem very harsh, but at any rate this is a very sensitive matter and I regret to be unable to give him the assurance he is asking for.
On the other hand, I can assure him that I shall consider with a great deal of attention the remarks he made tonight.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ATLANTIC REGION-STEPS TO IMPROVE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION

speechtext: Deputy Speaker: The hon. member for Queens.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-ATLANTIC REGION-STEPS TO IMPROVE UNEMPLOYMENT SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note that neither the Minister of Labour nor his parliamentary secretary is present. I assume this is inadvertent rather than studied discourtesy. I will address myself to one of the minister's colleagues, in this case.
Time after time we have read with anxiety and concern the unemployment figures which reveal that in the Atlantic area the unemployment index stands at twice the national average. Figures released today show 10.9 as against 3.2 and 3.4 for Ontario and for the 
Prairies. These regional disparities are not and should not be the concern of only those who come from the Atlantic region; they should be of concern to the whole national economy.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
As the Economic Council so rightly points out in page after page, it is one of their great priorities, as they see it, to do something to rectify the imbalance. So, if the Prime Minister were here and recalled his admonition to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) to be grateful for what the government had done, we would say in reply that this is not one area which makes us burst with gratitude. There has been insufficient attention to this problem, and on occasion definite acts and actions have aggravated and exacerbated the difficulty, such as the closing down of the enamel heating plant at Charlottetown, the closing down of the naval training centres, and the failure to move with rapidity on the much heralded $25 million grant to the ailing mining industry of Cape Breton, something with which my colleagues from the other island have acquainted the house many, many times. I should not like to bewail the past, but to urge whichever minister is going to reply and is going to take an interest in this matter that he, or the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), set out in terms of high priority an effort to remove the Atlantic region from this painful and persistent economic inequity which we have undergone for so long. I should like him to move forward on many fronts in co-operation with his colleagues in an effort to do something about this chronic state of high unemployment.
I could suggest to him that he seek to motivate his colleague, the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve), to get ARDA finally off the ground. I could suggest that the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) finally move and make the whole region a designated area under his legislation.
I might suggest, too, let us use a little imagination and realize that certain antiinflationary measures in other parts of the country are just as possible of being helpful to the Atlantic region. We need further acceleration of certain building projects. This is something that can be done without alteration to legislation, but with a little more common sense in administration. We want building projects further accelerated, not retarded; and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. March 17, 1966	COMMONS
Mcllraith) could be very helpful in this regard. We would like national establishments to be centred more in the Atlantic region, and the federal government can assist in the decentralization of industry. I should like more attention paid to our natural trading advantages.
Finally I invite the government to look upon this very painful situation, this blot upon the economic fagade of a great and prosperous country, and to call in others. This is a great government for conference and inquiry. I ask that it get together with the Atlantic premiers, who are setting a fine pattern of co-operation. I should like the government to call a meeting with the premiers, with the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council and the Atlantic Development Board, which should have a great increase in its capital fund. I should like them to call a meeting with the appropriate ministers of the Atlantic region, and there are only three of them now. I should like to see the minister look upon this one area as something in connection with which he, in his term of office, can show imaginative leadership and vigorous action. In this way he may do something about it, so that month after month we will not find the Atlantic provinces, where confederation began and whose presence in this was absolutely necessary, with these economic inequities under which we have laboured for 98 years.
I hope the minister will show some appreciative and appreciable area of amelioration and call upon the government to do these things. I am not interested in the Atlantic region aspect. I do not make comparisons with the circumstances of 1957, although they could be made; but I do say, in the name of the Atlantic region and, more particularly, in the name of a strong united Canada: Let us have some action.

Therefore, I shall set aside the remarks that were made and simply try to give a few ideas I have on the subject.
Among them, one I feel is of such significance, that among problems facing Canada some could, at a given time, bring about the dislocation of the country. Among these are not only the language problems and the problems of relations between ethnic groups, there are also the economic problems.
Canada, to my mind, cannot survive with areas not progressing at the same rate, or nearly at the same rate if you will, as the overall prosperity manifest in the rest of the country. In other words, for a country to hold together, the spread between the lowest and highest incomes must not be too large, as otherwise dislocation eventually occurs.
When the Maritimes are mentioned, I think it is justified, but a large part of Quebec should also be included, I mean everything south and east of Quebec City which economically, is more closely related to the economy of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island than to the general economy of Montreal and Ontario.
In any case, we really have a major problem here and I do not know what the budget holds in store for us, since even when you are a member of the cabinet, you are not told about all the secrets contained in the budget.
I do hope that the budget will take into account the points that were made and which, in my opinion, were very sound.
